explanations.B: Correct. The task is repeatable, its inputs are well defined, the output is easy to verify and a human reviews it before it goes anywhere. It's low consequence and reversible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Unattended credential rotation in production can cause outages, and it's hard to reverse quickly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Consequential decisions about people require human judgement and accountability. They shouldn't be automated.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Deletion is irreversible, and "no reads" doesn't prove data isn't needed (backups, compliance archives).

questions.scenario: A finance coordinator used Cowork to turn a folder of expense exports into an Excel budget summary with working formulas. The file opens without errors and will be sent to the finance director this afternoon.
questions.question: What should the coordinator do before sending it?

options.A: Send it, since Cowork produces spreadsheets with working formulas and the file opened and recalculated without errors.
options.B: Spot-check key totals and formulas against the source exports, and confirm any assumptions Cowork made (such as category mappings).
options.C: Convert it to PDF so nobody can see the formulas.
options.D: Ask Cowork to re-check its own formulas, add a "Verified" note to the header, and then send the file.
options.E: Delete the source exports so there is only one version of the truth.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Formulas can reference the wrong range or apply a wrong mapping and still calculate without errors.
explanations.B: Correct. Material sent to decision-makers needs spot-checks against the source data and review of any assumptions behind the numbers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hiding formulas reduces transparency and does nothing to make them correct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A self-check plus a label isn't independent verification against the source data, and it may give false assurance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Deleting the source data makes later verification impossible.

questions.scenario: A team's Claude Code usage costs have doubled this quarter. Investigation shows long sessions mixing unrelated tasks, and an 800-line CLAUDE.md that includes rarely used deployment procedures.
questions.question: Which TWO changes will most directly reduce token usage without hurting quality? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Use Agent Teams for every task so the work finishes faster.
options.B: Use /clear between unrelated tasks so each starts with focused context.
options.C: Move rarely used procedures out of CLAUDE.md into Skills that load only when needed.
options.D: Paste the whole repository into the first prompt so Claude never has to search.
options.E: Set effort to max for all tasks so fewer retries are needed.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Agent Teams use significantly more tokens than a single session.
explanations.B: Correct. Clearing context between unrelated tasks avoids paying for irrelevant history on every turn, which the cost guidance recommends.
explanations.C: Correct. CLAUDE.md loads every session. Moving occasional procedures into on-demand Skills is a documented token-reduction strategy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This inflates context and cost and buries relevant information.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Max effort raises token use on every task, including simple ones that don't benefit.

questions.scenario: An engineer starts a long verification task in Claude Code on their laptop. It needs the laptop's VPN access and local credentials. They have to leave for a meeting but want to watch progress and approve steps from their phone.
questions.question: Which option fits best?

options.A: Start a cloud session with claude --cloud so the task keeps running on Anthropic's infrastructure even while the laptop is closed for the meeting.
options.B: Create a routine that reruns the verification every hour and posts the results somewhere the phone can see.
options.C: Enable Remote Control for the local session and connect from the Claude mobile app, keeping the laptop's claude process running.
options.D: Move the task into Cowork.
options.E: Export the conversation to an Artifact and continue from it on the phone.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A cloud session clones the GitHub repository into a cloud environment and wouldn't have the laptop's VPN access or local credentials.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Routines run autonomously in the cloud on a schedule. They don't continue this interactive local session with its local credentials.
explanations.C: Correct. Remote Control lets you monitor and steer a session that keeps running locally, with local files and credentials, from another device. The local process must stay alive.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cowork targets knowledge-work tasks on the desktop. It doesn't give mobile control over a running Claude Code session.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An Artifact is a static or interactive output. It can't control a running coding session.

questions.scenario: Claude Code keeps suggesting a configuration syntax that a library deprecated in a release published after the model's training data. The generated code fails at startup.
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Keep regenerating until Claude happens to produce the new syntax.
options.B: Raise the effort level and ask Claude to reason step by step about how the library's API has most probably evolved since its training data was collected.
options.C: Switch to an older model, since it was trained when the library was more widely discussed and may know it better.
options.D: Tell Claude it is wrong without saying what changed.
options.E: Give Claude the current docs or changelog for the pinned version (pasted, fetched or via MCP), and record the version and syntax in CLAUDE.md or a rule.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The model lacks the information. Regenerating samples the same outdated knowledge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reasoning can't recover facts the model never saw. It produces more confident guesses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An older model has an even earlier cutoff and knows even less about the new release.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Corrections without specifics leave Claude guessing.
explanations.E: Correct. Supplying current, authoritative context fills the knowledge-cutoff gap. Recording it in project instructions stops the problem from coming back.

questions.scenario: A product manager asks an engineer to build "a dashboard for release health". The request has no metrics, data sources, users or edge cases. The engineer wants Claude Code to help turn it into something buildable without guessing.
questions.question: Which TWO approaches are most effective? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Tell Claude to make reasonable assumptions, document them in the README, and build the complete dashboard right away so stakeholders can react to it.
options.B: Keep the request vague, but select the most capable model at high effort so it can infer what the product manager most likely means.
options.C: Ask Claude to build five different dashboards and let stakeholders pick one later.
options.D: Ask Claude to interview you in detail about users, metrics, data sources, edge cases and trade-offs before writing anything.
options.E: Have Claude write a self-contained spec (files, interfaces, out-of-scope items, an end-to-end check), review it, then implement it in a fresh session.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Building on unstated assumptions produces a result that may not match what the product manager needed. That is expensive rework.
explanations.B: Incorrect. No model can recover requirements nobody has stated. Missing context needs to be gathered, not guessed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Five unguided builds multiply cost without clarifying the requirements and push decisions to the end.
explanations.D: Correct. The Claude Code best-practices guide recommends having Claude interview you for larger features. This surfaces implementation, UX, edge-case and trade-off questions you may not have considered.
explanations.E: Correct. A precise, self-contained spec with an end-to-end verification step, executed in a clean session, is the recommended follow-through after the interview.

questions.scenario: A marketing coordinator will use Cowork to draft personalised emails to 40 event partners from a contacts spreadsheet and send them through a connected email account. The laptop also holds payroll files in another folder.
questions.question: Which setup is most appropriate?

options.A: Connect the whole home directory so Claude can find any contact details it needs, and use Skip mode so the run isn't interrupted.
options.B: Connect the whole home directory and use Auto mode, since it blocks dangerous actions.
options.C: Connect only the event folder, and use the Manual approval mode so each send can be reviewed before it happens.
options.D: Use Skip mode but ask Claude in the prompt to be careful.
options.E: Share the live Cowork session with a colleague so they can watch it send emails.

explanations.A: Incorrect. This grants unnecessary access to sensitive files and removes all automatic checks. Skip is meant only for situations of complete trust.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Auto mode's self-review helps, but it doesn't justify exposing unrelated sensitive files. Outbound emails to partners warrant explicit review.
explanations.C: Correct. Least-privilege folder access keeps payroll data out of scope, and Manual approval puts a human checkpoint on each external, irreversible send.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A prompt request isn't a control. Skip removes the checks.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cowork doesn't support sharing a session with other users, and watching isn't the same as approving.

questions.scenario: A team wants Claude Code to read Jira tickets and post short status messages to a Slack channel during its workflow. Security wants control over which external actions are possible.
questions.question: Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Put the Jira API token in CLAUDE.md so Claude can authenticate without anyone needing to paste it in each session.
options.B: Connect the external services through MCP servers so Claude Code can use their tools.
options.C: Write a Skill describing the Jira and Slack APIs; a Skill on its own gives Claude the network access and credentials it needs.
options.D: Use permission rules that match MCP tools (for example mcp__jira__*) to allow, ask for or deny specific external actions.
options.E: Hooks are the only supported way for Claude Code to call external services.

explanations.A: Incorrect. CLAUDE.md is shared context, often committed to version control. Secrets must never go there.
explanations.B: Correct. MCP is the standard way to give Claude Code tools for external systems such as issue trackers and chat.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A Skill provides instructions and resources. It doesn't grant network access or authentication to external services.
explanations.D: Correct. Permission rules can target MCP tools by server or tool name, which gives security control over allowed external actions.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Hooks run commands on lifecycle events, but MCP is the primary integration path for external tools.

questions.scenario: Claude Code refactored a dashboard to remove duplication and improve naming. The brief required that behaviour stay the same, and the team lead must approve the merge.
questions.question: Which TWO pieces of evidence best show behaviour was preserved? (Select TWO.)

options.A: The total line count of the project went down, showing duplication was removed without adding new logic paths.
options.B: Claude states that behaviour is unchanged.
options.C: The existing test suite passes without the tests having been modified to fit the new code.
options.D: The new function and component names are more descriptive and match the conventions documented in CLAUDE.md.
options.E: Before-and-after browser checks of the core user flows match, with no new console errors.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fewer lines is a structural metric, not evidence that behaviour is preserved.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A completion claim isn't evidence.
explanations.C: Correct. Unchanged tests passing against refactored code is the main guardrail for a behaviour-preserving refactor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Better naming improves maintainability but says nothing about behaviour.
explanations.E: Correct. Runtime checks of the core flows catch UI and integration regressions that unit tests can miss.
